concepts.hook: Hesk's two hands, held open at the pole, carry the count of every knot she has wound into the string since Aun cut it.
*Mesket* kept her fire lit for nineteen winters after her husband's boat failed to come home, and each night she warmed one stone and set it by the empty place.
Old *Halmar* mended the village nets by lamplight, and her bone needle still stands above the pole, pulling the last loop tight.
Seven wooden pegs hold the string on Hesk's reel, one for each household that first lost a kite to the wind.
*Ennu* built the first kite-frame for his youngest sister from a split plank of wreck, and it hangs in the Spindle so that it can never blow away.
*Varo* carried an ember across the strait in a clay pot during the wet year, and her grandchildren still keep that pot glowing in the sky.
*Ithúna* notched a bone each time the water turned, and her bone rope now runs the length of the Spindle.
Two old fishers quarrelled for forty years and were buried under one sailcloth, and their two stars still share a single edge.
A child Hesk taught to tie a bowline in the dark, so the knot holds whether or not anyone is looking.
The half-tied loop Aun left on the string before his knife came down still hangs in the sky with its tail unpulled.
The stub of cut string that trails from the pole marks where the sky first came loose, and the elders touch it for luck before they count.
A stubborn nanny goat refused to be led out of a burning house, and her bell still rings faintly in the cold months.
*Skelra* split her oar to make a spar for the first sail mended at the hearth, and the household lived through the famine winter on what that sail brought home.
A bowl cracked and mended with sinew is passed from elder to elder, and each keeper adds one grain of salt before handing it on.
A mourning cloth hangs at the door of the house of *Oskel*, drowned in the spring, the first year that house had no man to go out in a boat.
A lamp is set on the sill each night for *Sil* the Drowned Lantern, so that she can find her way home to the house while she searches for Aun.
*Tessem*, a boy given the task of counting the names after the sickness, never got past the ninth hundred and the count is still open.
The warp of *Rahu*'s sailcloth loom, four hundred threads strung across the north, is still being woven by someone who is not yet born.
A father guides his son's hands through the old splice over his own, and the two of them are still working the same rope.
Smoke from the first fire of the house rises in a ring that never breaks, the circle of talk that goes on after the children are asleep.
*Mirra*'s cooking knife has been worn to a sliver by three generations of sharpening, and it is kept as the oldest tool in the Spindle.
Hesk's left hand rests on the pole while her right winds, so the star beneath that hand never moves because it is the rest.
A kite was made for a daughter who died before her first flight, and its tail of seabird feathers hangs forever unfurled above the hearth.
Two brothers who fell out each held one end of a line across the strait and never let go, and the line is still taut between their two stars.
A house burned its own boat boards to survive the long cold, and their embers make the warm stars of the north pole.
A round stone was pulled from Orrun's back by a fisher at low tide, and the house still wears it as an anchor against the wind.
Elders keep nine embers alight each night by an old rule, and whoever lets the ninth one die must tell the house before dawn.
Each infant receives a bone strung with its name at birth, and the bone is returned to the Reel when that person dies.
A widow's soup pot fed the whole village through the hungry year, and it is said to steam still, so that no house on the islands goes without.
Hesk once miscounted the knots and one star was left unfastened, so the Spindle has a single loose light that drifts in the wind and is never counted.
